title: Microbatch scheduler: token-aware fairness and request-level boundaries (draft)
content:
Goal / context:

This is a working draft exploring a continuous (micro)batching scheduler that reasons across token-level and request-level semantics. We want to 1) maximize GPU throughput with large, friendly kernel shapes, 2) respect per-request latency SLOs, and 3) enforce fairness (across tenants, routes, and priority classes) to avoid starvation and head-of-line delays.

Background / motivation:
- Our serving runtime benefits materially when the per-device kernels operate on consistent, aligned sequence lengths and when batches reach certain token counts (amortize kernel launch and memory overheads).
- Simple request-level batching (wait N requests or T ms) is easy but wastes opportunity: many requests produce tokens at different rates and lengths. Token-level continuous batching can pack tokens from multiple requests into GPU work and issue smaller but more frequent kernels with higher utilization.
- Tradeoffs: token-level packing improves GPU utilization and average throughput but complicates latency fairness, request accounting, kv-cache coherence, and kernel selection (different sequence lengths, attention work shapes).

High-level goals (prioritized):
- Meet per-request latency SLOs (p90/p99 targets configurable by route).
- Maximize GPU tokens/sec and throughput efficiency (minimize wasted compute due to padding and small kernels).
- Provide isolation and predictable fairness across customers and internal priority levels.
- Keep KV cache semantics consistent and avoid unnecessary flushes or duplication.
- Integrate cleanly with kernel-selector: prefer kernel shapes that align with batch shapes when possible.

Non-goals (for now):
- Replacing higher-level rollout policies (A/B) or doing cross-region routing.
- Solving model-level correctness differences.

Key concepts and vocabulary:
- microbatch: a unit of GPU work submitting many tokens (across requests) for one forward pass.
- request-level boundary: a full user request from initial prompt to EOS / stop; inference must maintain per-request ordering of tokens.
- token-slot: a logical slot representing the next token for a request in the microbatch. A request can occupy multiple token-slots across microbatches as it generates tokens.
- slot-age: time since a token-slot was admitted into the queue (useful for fairness).
- sequence-length-profile: runtime-maintained histogram of request prefix lengths and continuation lengths for kernel selection heuristics.

Design options considered (summary):
1) pure request-level batching: group whole requests up to N or T. Simple fairness: FIFO or weighted. Poor utilization for variable-length streaming workloads.
2) pure token-level continuous batching: pack available tokens into microbatches up to token budget. Great GPU utilization, complex fairness, requires per-token accounting and more kernel shapes.
3) hybrid / windowed token batching: operate token-level packing but enforce per-request latency budget and occasional request-level flushes (e.g., ceiling on how many microbatches a request can wait).

We recommend option 3 (hybrid) as the default: token-level packing for efficiency with request-aware backpressure and bounded waiting for fairness.

Scheduler components (roadmap):
- Admission controller: accepts new requests, assigns priority class, computes per-request deadlines and max-wait tokens.
- Token queue: hold token-slots with metadata (request id, priority, slot-age, model, route, kv-key).
- Microbatch builder: greedily or heuristically selects token-slots to form a microbatch (subject to token budget, kernel-shape constraints, fairness heuristic).
- Executor + kernel-selector: pick kernel variant given batch composition; submit to GPU runtime.
- Completion handler: updates request state (advance KV cache indices, per-request timers), emit metrics.

Admission and per-request invariants:
- Requests are admitted immediately; we create an initial token-slot for the first token generation. For streaming token-by-token flows, subsequent token-slots are enqueued as the request progresses.
- Each request gets a priority and a latency budget (configured per route). The admission controller attaches a per-request deadline = now + budget.
- The scheduler must ensure the request's next token is attempted before the deadline or trigger a fallback (e.g., proxy fallback, degrade to lower-quality but faster model variant) to preserve SLOs.

Microbatch formation: heuristics
- Hard token cap: set a max_tokens_per_microbatch (e.g., 4096 tokens) to limit kernel latency and memory.
- Kernel-alignment preference: prefer selecting tokens that produce similar attention sizes and key/value shapes to reuse kernels efficiently. The microbatch builder consults sequence-length-profile to prefer homogeneous groups.
- Age-first slice: reserve a fraction of microbatch slots for oldest token-slots (to avoid starvation). E.g., 20% of slots for oldest requests; 80% for throughput packing.
- Priority quotas: enforce per-priority or per-tenant token quotas over sliding windows (to prevent noisy-neighbor abuse).
- Max wait cap per-request: if a request's waiting time exceeds threshold W (configurable, typical 30–80ms for streaming), the scheduler will prioritize its slots in subsequent batches.

Token vs Request boundaries: practical rules
- Do not split a single token generation across multiple kernels: one token generation per token-slot maps to one kernel invocation for that position. But a request may have tokens spread across many microbatches as it generates outputs.
- Maintain per-request ordering: tokens from a request are emitted in sequence order, and we must not interleave beyond the natural token sequence. Interleaving across other requests is permitted as long as ordering within the request is preserved.
- For sampling-mode generation (top-k/top-p), we need the RNG/stream to be deterministic per-request; microbatch executor must ensure per-request RNG state is passed to kernels.

Fairness strategies (detailed):
1) Weighted Token Fair Queuing (WTFQ)
   - Maintain per-tenant/per-route virtual queues and allocate token budget per quantum proportional to weight.
   - Use token accounting: when building a microbatch, pick tokens to respect the virtual deficit counters (deficit round robin adapted to tokens).
   - Pros: strong fairness by token consumption; cons: more complex bookkeeping and can increase tail latency for small, high-priority requests unless combined with age bias.

2) Age-biased prioritized packing
   - Keep an overall token queue sorted by slot-age but allow bumping weight of high-priority classes.
   - When building a microbatch, fill remaining slots starting from oldest. This reduces p99 starvation.
   - Pros: simple to reason about; cons: may reduce throughput in adversarial mixes.

3) Hybrid: reserve headroom for SLO-sensitive requests
   - Reserve R tokens in every microbatch exclusively for requests whose deadlines are near. The remainder is filled for throughput.
   - Combine with per-tenant quotas to protect capacity.

We propose hybrid: WTFQ + age bias + reserved SLO tokens. Practical numbers to tune: reserve 12-25% of tokens for SLO-near slots; min-batch-fill for throughput at 75-88%.

KV cache interaction and consistency:
- KV caches (per request) live in GPU memory. When microbatching tokens from multiple requests, we must gather correct KV pointers per request and ensure alignment for batched kernels.
- Implementation note: use gather/scatter indirection arrays passed to kernels describing request->kv-index mapping. Kernel variants should accept per-slot kv-index arrays to read the correct KV slices. This avoids copying/cache duplication.
- Cache pressure: token-level packing tends to interleave many request KV caches on the same device; track per-request KV working set size and prefer microbatches that keep working sets compact to reduce page thrashing.
- Eviction policy: when per-device memory pressure is high, evict least-recently-used request KV slices but annotate request as 'kv-miss' so executor can rehydrate partial KV from host memory (costly but acceptable for infrequent cases).

Kernel selection complexities:
- Kernels are tuned for certain sequence-length / key-value shapes (e.g., short-prefix optimized, long-prefix optimized, quantized kernels). Microbatch builder should prefer tokens whose combined shapes match an existing fast kernel.
- If the chosen tokens create a heterogenous shape, kernel-selector can choose a generic slower kernel or split the microbatch into shape-homogeneous sub-microbatches (tradeoff launch overhead vs slower kernel).
- Heuristic: if more than P% of tokens match a dominant shape, pick that kernel and pad others; otherwise split into two microbatches. P is tunable (start at 70%).

Backpressure and client-visible signals:
- We must expose approximate queueing delay metrics via the API (e.g., X-ms estimated headroom) or provide explicit SLO hints in SDK so client can opt-in to lower-latency mode.
- If admission backlog grows beyond thresholds, return 429/Retry-After for low-priority routes or route requests to fallback models.

Metrics to emit (essential):
- tokens/sec per-device, per-model, per-tenant
- microbatch_size distribution (tokens and slots)
- kernel_shape utilization and padding overhead (%)
- per-request wait time histogram (p50/p90/p99) and number of microbatches consumed per request
- KV cache hit/miss rates and rehydration latency
- fairness metrics: per-tenant normalized token share vs weight

Safety & operational knobs:
- Configurable max_tokens_per_microbatch and max_kernel_latency_ms (safety cap on single kernel time)
- Per-route latency budget defaults; route owners can opt-in to low-latency mode that reduces batching aggressiveness
- Emergency fallback: when observed p99 latency exceeds threshold, auto-shrink microbatch sizes and raise SLO-reserved tokens to 50% until stabilized.

Open questions / TODOs:
- How to expose deterministic per-request RNG seeds and ensure reproducibility across microbatches? (need API-level seed and kernel contract).
- How to allocate memory for billions of tiny KV slices when tenancy is high? Consider compacting KV slices into pooled pages with per-request offsets.
- Benchmark plan: synthetic mix + production trace replay. Need tooling to replay token-arrival patterns and measure p50/p99 tradeoffs across hybrid policies.
- Interaction with quantized kernel paths: some kernels expect fixed tile sizes; how to generalize gather/scatter approach?
- Potential for per-model learned batching policy using RL or bandits to adapt batch heuristics by workload. Low priority but interesting.

Prototype algorithm (pseudocode):
1) admission(request): assign priority, deadline, kv-pointer; append initial token-slot to global token_queue.
2) periodic microbatch_worker wake (target interval 8–20ms):
   a) collect list of SLO-near slots (deadline < now + margin), reserve R tokens from budget for them
   b) from global token_queue, select up to R tokens by age/prio for SLO slots
   c) fill remaining budget by:
       i) pick dominant kernel-shape candidates (consult profile)
       ii) greedily pack tokens that match shape and respect per-tenant quotas/weights
       iii) if leftover heterogenous tokens exist beyond threshold, either pad or split microbatch
   d) lock-per-device and submit built microbatch to executor with per-slot metadata (kv-index, rng-seed, request-id)

Notes on fairness bookkeeping: maintain per-tenant deficit counters updated on token consumption and a sliding-window total tokens. Use decay to let long-term weights apply.

Experiment matrix (initial):
- workloads: 1) many short (2–6 token) streaming requests; 2) mix short and long; 3) bursty single-tenant; 4) multi-tenant noisy neighbor.
- policies: request-only batching, token-only, hybrid (with reserve fractions 12/25/50), WTFQ vs age-biased.
- targets: measure tokens/sec, p50/p90/p99 latency, kernel padding overhead, KV-miss rate.

Implementation checklist (milestones):
- [ ] simple token_queue + microbatch worker, naive FIFO packing (MVP)
- [ ] per-request deadline enforcement and SLO-reserved slots
- [ ] integrate kernel-selector hints (sequence-length-profile)
- [ ] per-tenant quotas and WTFQ prototype
- [ ] KV gather/scatter kernel interface and memory accounting
- [ ] load tests and trace replay harness

Notes-to-self / rough ideas:
- Might be useful to model the scheduler as two interleaved flows: SLO-critical fast-path with small microbatches and high-priority kernels, and throughput path that aggregates remaining tokens into large, optimized kernels.
- Consider making the microbatch interval adaptive: shorter intervals under low load to reduce latency, longer to build bigger batches when backlog exists.
- Expose an "interactive" flag in the API that opts requests into SLO-reserved path. SDK should default to interactive for streaming UX.

References / prior art:
- research papers on scheduling for packet switching (WRR, DRR) adapted to tokens
- recent serving papers showing token-level batching for autoregressive models (internal lab notes)

Next steps:
- Validate baseline with replay traces (ENG-9876)
- Build MVP FIFO-token microbatching and test microbench kernels for gather/scatter overhead
- Sync with kernel team on shape-annotations required in microbatch metadata (meeting with Marta next week)

End of draft.

-- Priya
